hints: Think about what makes any O-H acid strong: how easily it loses $H^+$ and how stable the negative ion left behind is.
Sort the four into two families first, the two carboxylic acids versus phenol versus ethanol, by comparing $RCOO^-$ with phenoxide and ethoxide.
Within the two carboxylic acids, compare $ClCH_2COOH$ with $CH_3COOH$ by looking at what Cl does to electron density compared with an alkyl group.
Compare phenol with ethanol by asking where the lone pair on oxygen can go in phenoxide but cannot go in ethoxide.
walkthrough:
Set the rule for acidity**
Picture each acid losing $H^+$: $HA \rightarrow H^+ + A^-$. The more stable $A^-$ is, the more the equilibrium lies to the right and the stronger the acid. So you are really comparing stabilities of carboxylate ions, phenoxide ion and ethoxide ion.

Place carboxylic acids at the top**
Carboxylate ions, $RCOO^-$, spread the negative charge over two oxygen atoms by delocalisation: $R-C(O^-)=O \leftrightarrow R-C(O)=O^-$. Phenoxide spreads charge into the ring but less effectively, and ethoxide keeps the full charge on one oxygen. That gives acids > phenol > ethanol as a first grouping.

Split the two carboxylic acids with inductive effects**
In $ClCH_2COOH$, chlorine is very electronegative and pulls electron density toward itself through sigma bonds. This negative inductive effect pulls charge away from $COO^-$, stabilising it and weakening the $O-H$ bond. In $CH_3COOH$, the $CH_3$ group pushes electrons toward $COO^-$, which slightly destabilises it. So $ClCH_2COOH$ is stronger.

Split phenol and ethanol**
In phenol, the oxygen lone pair overlaps with the benzene pi system, so in $C_6H_5O^-$ the negative charge is delocalised into the ring. In ethanol, there is no ring, and the ethyl group donates electrons by positive inductive effect, intensifying the negative charge on $CH_3CH_2O^-$ and making it very unstable. Hence phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol, giving the final order $ClCH_2CO_2H > CH_3CO_2H > C_6H_5OH > C_2H_5OH$.

Final answer: chloroethanoic acid > ethanoic acid > phenol > ethanol (most to least acidic).
Greater acidity is due to weakening of the $O-H$ bond and stabilisation of the anion formed.
$ClCH_2CO_2H$ > $CH_3CO_2H$ due to electronegative Cl withdrawing electrons by negative inductive effect, stabilising $ClCH_2COO^-$.
$CH_3CO_2H$ > phenol due to electron withdrawing $C=O$ stabilising $CH_3COO^-$ by delocalisation over two O atoms.
Phenol > ethanol as the lone pair on O in phenoxide is delocalised into the benzene ring, while in ethanol the alkyl group donates electrons by positive inductive effect, destabilising $CH_3CH_2O^-$.

hints: Recall what warm acidified $MnO_4^-$ does to a reducing agent: think oxidation, and what colour change purple $MnO_4^-$ to colourless $Mn^{2+}$ looks like.
Work out the carbon oxidation state in $HOOC-COOH$ and in $CO_2$ to see why only $CO_2$ and $H_2O$ can be the products.
walkthrough:
Spot oxidation**
Warm acidified $KMnO_4$ is a powerful oxidising agent. Ethanedioic acid, $HOOC-COOH$, is a good reducing agent that is easily oxidised right up to $CO_2$ where carbon is at its maximum oxidation state of +4.

Link colour to observation**
$MnO_4^-(aq)$ is intensely purple. When it oxidises something else it is itself reduced to $Mn^{2+}(aq)$ which is colourless / very pale pink. Because excess acid is present, all the purple disappears. At the same time $CO_2$ gas bubbles out, so you see effervescence.

Write the simplest equation**
Using $[O]$ to represent the oxidising agent keeps it simple: $$HOOC-COOH + [O] \rightarrow 2CO_2 + H_2O$$ Check atoms: $C_2H_2O_4$ on the left plus one O gives $C_2H_2O_5$, and $2CO_2 + H_2O$ is $C_2H_2O_5$. Balanced. The full ionic version is $$5HOOC-COOH + 2MnO_4^- + 6H^+ \rightarrow 10CO_2 + 8H_2O + 2Mn^{2+}$$

Final answer: type of reaction: oxidation (ethanedioic acid is oxidised).
observations: purple solution decolourises to colourless / very pale pink, effervescence due to $CO_2$.
equation: $HOOC-COOH + [O] \rightarrow 2CO_2 + H_2O$

hints: Mark every ester $C(O)-O$ link in Fig. 8.1 and imagine adding $H_2O$ back across each one to regenerate $C(O)OH$ and $HO-C$.
Look at the two different alcohol fragments, $O-CH_2-$ and $O-CH(CH_3)-$, to see that two different hydroxyacids must be involved.
walkthrough:
Reverse condensation**
A polyester forms by $C(O)OH + HO-C \rightarrow C(O)-O-C + H_2O$. To find monomers, cut each $C(O)-O$ bond in Fig. 8.1 and put $OH$ back on the carbonyl carbon and $H$ back on the oxygen.

Collect the fragments**
Cutting $$-O-CH_2-C(O)-O-CH(CH_3)-C(O)-$$ gives $HO-CH_2-C(O)-OH$, which is $HOCH_2C(O)OH$, and $HO-CH(CH_3)-C(O)-OH$, which is $CH_3CH(OH)C(O)OH$. The chain is alternating, so only these two hydroxyacids are needed. Each contains both $OH$ and $CO_2H$, so each can self condense but here they co-polymerise.

Final answer: Monomer 1: $HOCH_2C(O)OH$ (2-hydroxyethanoic acid / glycolic acid).
Monomer 2: $CH_3CH(OH)C(O)OH$ (2-hydroxypropanoic acid / lactic acid).

hints: Remember a polypeptide uses only the $NH_2$ and $CO_2H$ of serine, the side chain $CH_2OH$ stays unchanged, so join $C(O)OH$ of one to $H_2N$ of the next with loss of $H_2O$.
Draw the amide link displayed as $-C(O)-NH-$ and keep the alpha carbon with its $H$ and $CH_2OH$ intact, adding continuation bonds at both ends for two units.
walkthrough:
Choose the correct functional groups**
Serine is $H_2N-CH(CH_2OH)-C(O)OH$. For a polypeptide, ignore the side chain $CH_2OH$. React the carboxyl of one molecule with the amino of the next: $C(O)OH + H_2N \rightarrow C(O)-NH + H_2O$.

Build two repeat units**
Line up two serines head to tail: $$---NH-CH(CH_2OH)-C(O)-NH-CH(CH_2OH)-C(O)---$$ Show the peptide group fully displayed as $-C(=O)-N(H)-$, keep each alpha $C$ tetrahedral with $H$ and $CH_2OH$, and put short continuation bonds through the terminal $NH$ and $C(O)$ to show the chain continues.

Final answer: Polypeptide with two serine residues: $---NH-CH(CH_2OH)-C(O)-NH-CH(CH_2OH)-C(O)---$ with continuation bonds at each end and the peptide $C(O)-NH$ linkage shown displayed. Side chain $CH_2OH$ unchanged on each alpha carbon.

hints: Compare the polar $C(O)-O$ and $C(O)-N$ links in condensation polymers with the non-polar all carbon backbone of addition polymers, and ask which can be attacked by water or enzymes.
walkthrough:
Focus on the link that water can break**
Think of biodegradation as hydrolysis by water or enzymes in the environment. Ester links, $-C(O)-O-$, and amide / peptide links, $-C(O)-NH-$, are polar and easily attacked by water to regenerate acid plus alcohol or amine. Addition polymers like poly(ethene) contain only strong non-polar $C-C$ and $C-H$ bonds with no site for water to attack, so they persist much longer.

Final answer: Condensation polymers contain polar ester or amide linkages that can be hydrolysed by water / acids / enzymes, whereas addition polymers have an inert hydrocarbon backbone of $C-C$ bonds that cannot be hydrolysed.
